ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: As shown in the figure, the mathematics interest group measures the height of the flagpole $CD$ and the academic building $AB$. Firstly, at point E, they use an altimeter $EF$ of 1.5 meters high to measure the elevation angle of the top of the academic building A, $\angle AFH$, as $45^\circ$. At this moment, the top of the flagpole D is exactly in line with sight $FA$. Then, moving forward 12 meters to point G (G is on $CD$), the elevation angle of the top of the academic building A, $\angle AGH$, is measured as $60^\circ$. Points B, C, and E are on the same horizontal line. Find the height of the academic building $AB$ (express the result as an exact value).
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text:
\textbf{Solution:} Let GH = x meters. Given that AB$\parallel$DC$\parallel$EF, EF = CG = BH, and $\angle$ABE = $90^\circ$, \\
$\therefore$ the quadrilateral BCGH is a rectangle, $\therefore$ $\angle$AHF = DGF = $90^\circ$. From (1), we have: DG = FG = 12 meters, BH = EF = 1.5 meters, \\
$\because$ $\angle$AFH = $45^\circ$, $\therefore$ $\triangle$AFH is an isosceles right triangle, \\
$\therefore$ AH = FH, $\because$ $\angle$AGH = $60^\circ$, $\therefore$ $\tan$ $\angle$AGH = $\frac{AH}{GH} = \tan60^\circ = \sqrt{3}$, \\
$\therefore$ AH = $\sqrt{3}$GH = $\sqrt{3}x$ (meters), \\
$\because$ FH = GH + FG = (x + 12) meters, $\therefore$ $\sqrt{3}x = x + 12$, \\
Solving gives: x = $6\sqrt{3}+6$, $\therefore$ GH = ($6\sqrt{3}+6$) meters, AH = (18 + $6\sqrt{3}$) meters, \\
$\therefore$ AB = BH + AH = (19.5 + $6\sqrt{3}$) meters, \\
Therefore, the height of the teaching building AB is \boxed{19.5+6\sqrt{3}} meters.
